> Every default is set in the client and/or in the schemas.

Small subtlety: while I agree what you write is true, it also uses a particular definition of what a default is that may not initially be obvious. Here, a default is the literal value assigned to a field in the schema, and all fields in the input schema have a default value. Therefore if you omit a field, its eventual value is not a property of the service version, but rather of the schema.

_However_, maybe the best example to focus on here is chunk size. The default value is the string literal `"auto"`. So in this sense, the default value of the field means that you opt-in to whatever the service version wants you to do that day. I like this because it's very explicit. It's rather different than, say, a field ` foo: bool` with no default value, that gets assigned by the service when omitted. Rather, we would need to do `foo: bool | Literal["choose_for_me"]` if we wanted this behaviour.

> [@jyu00](https://github.com/jyu00)
> 
> > What is the alternative you plan to use? It was first introduced to differentiate None (a valid value) and "use server default".
> 
> With Executor and NLV3, we have shifted to a new paradigm where there are no more server defaults, for transparency. Every default is set in the client and/or in the schemas. Therefore, `Unset` is no longer useful in these newer option classes

This was the behavior we had in V1 primitives. We switched to "using server defaults" in V2 because, iirc, people argued that if you're calling a service, the default values should be based on the service version, not the client version you're using. Similar to what Ian said, it also gives the added benefit of knowing (although imperfectly) whether a value is explicitly requested by the user, or they're fine taking whatever the server default is.

After verifying the API fix worked, I'm re-targeting this PR for mostly some cleanups.

For future reference, we still handle "jobs cancelled due to exceeding specified max time" as a particular case, considering them [ERROR instead of CANCELLED](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/blob/0.46.1/qiskit_ibm_runtime/runtime_job_v2.py#L179-L180) and having a dedicated `RuntimeJobMaxTimeoutError` exception. The first bit is inconsistent with how the API signals them - and it can be argued that the current behavior was an explicit decision by the client (`.error_message()` can be interpreted as only available for jobs that error, and changing the status might be a breaking change in some scenarios).

So I'm considering tackling that out of the scope of this PR (original for catching a bug, now for some non-breaking cleanup), and prefer to revise this particular case as part of a bigger revision that can be included in 1.0.

In general, the recommended flow is to open an issue describing the bug / feature / enhancement so the maintainers can comment on the need, prioritize/plan if needed, and provide feedback before starting work (through a PR). This flow is mainly a communication / coordination vehicle, for maximizing alignment and preventing duplicated (or extra) work, and is to be taken as a general rule (it is fine to deviate in specific occasions such as smaller bits as this PR or your previous one!).

Regarding adding validation for empty circuits - if the intent is to have a check inside `NoiseLearner.run()` raising an exception if no circuits are passed, I'd actually suggest _not_ going for it.

It might seem counter-intuitive (and we are not too consistent in the codebase in that regard) when it comes to usability, but the approach is placing trust in the users and guiding through type hints and documentation for the function's behavior and meaning of arguments in general. Fine-grained and abundant validation has a maintenance cost (ie. it can be argued that if there is a check for empty pubs, we should also check for the validity of every item, for extra conditions, to extend it to all primitives, etc) that has a chance of restricting users' freedom and extensibility without providing too much value _if_ we are able to guide the user correctly through other means.

I can reproduce that behavior locally: and it seems it can be explained at least partially due to timing. As the script exits almost immediately, the underlying `future` (created [here](https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit/blob/main/qiskit/primitives/primitive_job.py#L54-L56)) likely does not have time to start running, which leads to graceful shutdown as the script ends. Can you try adding a `sleep(1)` after the `print` statement, and comment back on the script and notebook behavior? Locally (and testing on the script), that extra time makes the `future` able to start running - so the script execution does not end until the simulator execution ends.

I'm also wondering about the use case: you are creating a `job`, but not waiting for it to finish (usually via `job.result()`). Waiting for the result to be available would ensure your "session" (as in, the script or the notebook) is alive until the simulation is completed.

- Changing name, as suggested in other comments
- Placing `sampler_v2` inside a subfolder `executor_routines` (name can be improved). This would give us a natural container to place functions that need to be used by both wrapper-sampler and wrapper-estimator, such as the DD pass (@TsafrirA , do we expect any other function to be "shared"?)

Since the behavior still seems stochastic, what do you think would be the best fix for this ? Thanks for checking - at a first look, it does seem to point to an out of memory issue. Simulators are very demanding in terms of memory (you can find more details in [this documentation page](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/guides/debugging-tools)), with tight correlation with the number of qubits (and it seems you are using `ibm_kingston`, which is a 156 qubit device), and your job might just be too demanding (for the record, locally when I added the extra delay for ensuring the simulator has enough time to kick in and the `future` to start running, I did not wait for the job to finish, killed the process).

A suggestion for approaching validating and debugging using simulators would be to try to start with a simpler version of the problem (as hinted in the linked documentation page: smaller circuits if applicable, smaller devices if applicable), and scale up to the full version of the problem using a real device. Regardless, you will always find simulators useful for just a subset of purposes (they don't provide the same features as a real device as you experienced, and are not practical for large workloads), and you are bound to hit some limits inherent to simulators - so when designing an experiment, it is usually worth to plan around the differences between simulator and devices accordingly.

Other suggestions that might help:
* you might find the [fake providers](https://quantum.cloud.ibm.com/docs/en/api/qiskit-ibm-runtime/fake-provider) convenient for your needs. In general, we encourage using them instead of an `AerSimulator` instance directly. It adds a few layers in between when it comes to submission, but might streamline your workflow.
* if you suspect the segmentation fault / double free or corruption might come from a `qiskit-aer` bug, I would encourage coming up with a simpler reproducible example and inspecting the core dump, and reaching out to Aer maintainers throw an issue in their repo.
* a (sketchy) look into what happens when using `Estimator.run()` with a simulator backend is:
   1. `qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider.local_service.QiskitRuntimeService::_run_backend_primitive_v2()` is the last layer in this package that is responsible for signalling that the job is to be run
   2. `qiskit.primitives.backend_estimator_v2.BackendEstimatorV2::run()` creates and submits the job, ultimately running `qiskit.primitives.backend_estimator_v2._run_circuits()` inside a `future`
   3. if using a `FakeBackend`, `qiskit_ibm_runtime.fake_provider.fake_backend.FakeBackendV2::run()` is invoked, which delegates into `AerSimulator` 
   4. `qiskit_aer.backends.aer_simulator.AerSimulator::run()` performs the actual simulation

   This is mostly a pointer for pieces that might help diagnose further or provide you with more control. As technical notes, `future`s are usually [not cancellable](https://docs.python.org/3/library/concurrent.futures.html#concurrent.futures.Future.cancel) once they start running and are integral part of the current approach - which makes changing the overall model quite involved.

I still wonder about the specific of the use case (thanks for the insight!): if you are not making use of the result of the job, I wonder if you do need to create a job at all in your scenario (which would bypass the need for graceful termination or memory issues). Pretty much all the workflows assume that if an user is submitting a job (locally or remotely), that job will be waited for and the results used one way or the other (so keeping the script or notebook until a job is completed, and managing the job complexity and ensuring it can be simulated in the user local environment are in practice delegated to the user domain) - supporting such an edge use case might be outside scope.

> The task is to add similar support to `reset_2` (mid-circuit single qubit reset) and `measure_reset` (I think it's a mid-circuit measurement followed immediately by a reset on the same qubit).

To add more context, `reset_2` is a conditional reset that uses `measure_2` to do the measurement and flip the qubit state based on that outcome. It's useful for mid-circuit reset for the same reason `measure_2` is (shorter circuit). 

`measure_reset` is the same as `reset_2`, except it also returns the measurement outcome. This is a faster operation than doing an explicit measurement + conditional reset.

For `ConvertMidCircuitMeasureReset`, I guess the idea is to replace something like

```python
circuit.measure(q0, c0)
with circuit.if_test((c0, 1)):
    circuit.x(q0)
```

with 

```python
circuit.append(MidCircuitMeasureReset(), q0, c0)
```

If we want a common pass, I'd suggest making this conversion optional, since it changes more than just a simple `measure/reset` -> `measure_2/reset_2`.

This comes from https://github.com/Qiskit/qiskit-ibm-runtime/pull/2843#discussion_r3314151188, and probably boils down to the concept of `correct`.

As there is only one file at the moment, I advocated for not creating an extra folder, and just place it in the parent folder. It is the same approach we use in other places (for example, `test_execution_span.py`): even if `foo` is a module that has `foo.bar` and `foo.baz`, if the test is reasonably small, we just start by `test_foo.py` and later decide if it merits converting to `foo/test_bar.py` and `foo/test_baz.py`. 

From my point of view, it saves us some nesting churn and is more evident / effective, so that is my _subjective_ definition of "correct". I'll refrain from approving / rejecting in the hopes of a more unified definition of "correct", as I'm biased 😄
